title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Gonzalez launches statewide push for data center rules on power and water risks.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's a busy Wednesday morning across the state, and our big story today is Senator Gonzalez hitting the road on a new tour to build support for tighter oversight of these AI facilities.
That sounds like it could shape how a lot of these projects move forward or get reined in.
Exactly. The tour is highlighting risks to electric reliability and water supplies in rural and suburban spots where proposals keep popping up.
Why now? What's driving the push for these rules at the state level?
Residents are getting a direct chance to weigh in before more campuses get approved, and the senator is framing it around protecting local infrastructure.
I've been wondering how this fits with all the local pauses we've seen. Is this building on that momentum?
It seems that way. Communities have been using moratoria to buy time for studies, and now there's a statewide effort to set clearer standards.
What kind of rules are we talking about? Limits on size, water use, or power contracts?
The focus is on oversight that addresses electric reliability and water supplies, especially in areas that aren't set up for industrial-scale demand.
And how does that connect to people's electric bills?
Large facilities can strain the grid, and if new power isn't added fast enough, ratepayers often end up covering the upgrades through higher bills.
That makes sense. What about water? Are we talking about cooling systems that pull from local aquifers or rivers?
Yes, data centers use a lot for cooling, and in rural spots that can compete with farms and households, especially during dry spells.
Farmland is already taking hits from transmission lines too. How does this tour address that bigger picture?
The stops are meant to give folks in those areas a voice on where projects land and what protections are in place.
Who are the main players here besides the senator?
Local officials, residents, utilities, and developers are all watching closely as the tour moves through proposed sites.
What's the history of these fights in Michigan so far?
Towns have been extending bans while they study impacts, and lawsuits are starting to pop up over blocked projects.
How many places have paused already?
Quite a few across the state, from suburbs to rural counties, all trying to get ahead of the wave.
What happens next after these public stops?
The goal is to gather support for legislation that sets statewide guardrails before more approvals happen.
Could this lead to actual bills this session?
That's the hope — turning resident feedback into concrete proposals that balance growth with protections.
And for towns 30 or 60 miles away, why should they care?
Power and water don't respect city limits, so one big project can ripple out through rates and supply.
Any sense of how utilities are responding to the tour?
They're already dealing with surging demand from AI, so clearer rules could help them plan upgrades better.
What if the tour doesn't build enough support?
Then we might see more piecemeal local rules and continued uncertainty for everyone involved.
Sounds like a pivotal moment.
It really does. Let's keep an eye on how the stops go and what feedback comes back.
Moving to quick hits, East Lansing just extended its data center freeze for another year.
Right, the city council voted to keep the moratorium in place, blocking new applications while they study long-term impacts.
And residents 30 miles away in the Lansing region face the same risks if something lands nearby?
Exactly, so the extension keeps zoning rules steady in the meantime.
Next, a University of Michigan regent is urging a pause on the Ypsilanti Township proposal over grid strain.
Yes, highlighting electricity demand and local infrastructure costs that could lead to rate hikes without new safeguards.
Kalamazoo commissioners are set to decide on a six-month ban today.
That would halt new proposals and give time to write permanent rules before any project advances.
Michigan's AG is challenging an OpenAI-Oracle deal over costs to ratepayers.
Dana Nessel is pushing back on potential spikes in household electricity bills from that arrangement.
Corunna adopted new zoning rules for future data centers.
Those standards in Shiawassee County now set clearer limits on size and location to protect infrastructure.
University of Michigan locked in the Textile Road site for a big Los Alamos supercomputer campus.
The $1.2 billion project in Pittsfield Township will draw heavy power and water in Washtenaw County.
Yesterday a developer sued an Oakland County town after a project was blocked.
That lawsuit could reshape how property taxes and power costs are handled going forward.
Rochester Hills extended its ban another year amid power and water worries.
The suburb is studying impacts while keeping large proposals on hold.
And Consumers Energy transmission lines are sparking farm backlash.
Farmers are protesting lost land and property values tied to upgrades for data center demand.
On deck for today, Speaker Township Planning Commission meets on an ordinance covering cryptocurrency data mining, data centers including AI, and residential battery storage.
That's a chance for residents to weigh in directly on the rules.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Sen. Gonzalez Kicks Off Tour for Tighter Data Center Oversight
